{{short description|Identity expressing an integral as a sum}}
{{More footnotes needed|date=September 2025}}
{{Use shortened footnotes|date=May 2021}}

In mathematics, the '''sophomore's dream''' is the pair of [[identity (mathematics)|identities]] (especially the first)

<math display="block">\begin{alignat}{2}
  & \int_0^1 x^{-x}\,dx &&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-n} \\
  & \int_0^1 x^x   \,dx &&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n+1}n^{-n} = - \sum_{n=1}^\infty (-n)^{-n}
\end{alignat}</math>
discovered in 1697 by [[Johann Bernoulli]].

The numerical values of these constants are approximately 1.291285997... and 0.7834305107..., respectively.<!-- per OEIS, as in References -->

The name "sophomore's dream"<ref>It appears in {{Harvnb|Borwein|Bailey|Girgensohn|2004}}.</ref> is in contrast to the name "[[freshman's dream]]" which is given to the incorrect<ref group="note">Incorrect in general, but correct when one is working in a [[commutative ring]] of prime [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] {{mvar|p}} with {{mvar|n}} being a power of {{mvar|p}}. The correct result in a general commutative context is given by the [[binomial theorem]].</ref> identity {{nowrap|<math display="inline">(x+y)^n=x^n+y^n</math>.}} The [[Sophomore year|sophomore]]'s dream has a similar too-good-to-be-true feel, but is true.

== Proof ==

[[Image:Sophdream.png|thumb|right|200px|Graph of the functions ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sup>''x''</sup> (red, lower) and ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sup>&minus;''x''</sup> (grey, upper) on the interval ''x''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;(0,&nbsp;1&#93;.]]
The proofs of the two identities are completely analogous, so only the proof of the second is presented here.
The key ingredients of the proof are:
* to write <math display="inline">x^x = \exp(x\log x)</math> (using the notation {{math|log}} for the [[natural logarithm]] and {{math|exp}} for the [[exponential function]]);
* to expand <math display="inline">\exp(x\log x)</math> using the [[power series]] for {{math|exp}}; and
* to integrate termwise, using [[integration by substitution]].

In detail, {{math|''x''<sup>''x''</sup>}} can be expanded as

<math display="block">x^x = \exp(x \log  x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n(\log  x)^n}{n!}.</math>

Therefore,

<math display="block">\int_0^1 x^x\,dx =  \int_0^1 \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n(\log  x)^n}{n!} \,dx. </math>

By [[uniform convergence]] of the power series, one may interchange summation and integration to yield

<math display="block">\int_0^1 x^x\,dx = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{x^n(\log  x)^n}{n!} \,dx. </math>

To evaluate the above integrals, one may change the variable in the integral via the [[Integration by substitution|substitution]] <math display="inline">x=\exp(-\frac{u}{n+1}).</math>  With this substitution, the bounds of integration are transformed to <math>0 < u < \infty, </math> giving the identity
<math display="block">\int_0^1 x^n(\log x)^n\,dx = (-1)^n (n+1)^{-(n+1)}  \int_0^\infty u^n  e^{-u}\,du.</math>
By [[Euler integral|Euler's integral identity]] for the [[Gamma function#Definition|Gamma function]], one has  
<math display="block">\int_0^\infty u^n e^{-u}\,du=n!,</math>
so that
<math display="block">\int_0^1 \frac{x^n (\log  x)^n}{n!}\,dx
= (-1)^n (n+1)^{-(n+1)}.</math>

Summing these (and changing indexing so it starts at {{math|1= ''n'' = 1}} instead of {{math|1= ''n'' = 0}}) yields the formula.

=== Historical proof ===
The original proof, given in Bernoulli,{{sfn|Bernoulli|1697}} and presented in modernized form in Dunham,{{sfn|Dunham|2005}} differs from the one above in how the termwise integral <math display="inline">\int_0^1 x^n(\log x)^n\,dx</math> is computed, but is otherwise the same, omitting technical details to justify steps (such as termwise integration). Rather than integrating by substitution, yielding the Gamma function (which was not yet known), Bernoulli used [[integration by parts]] to iteratively compute these terms.

The integration by parts proceeds as follows, varying the two exponents independently to obtain a recursion. An indefinite integral is computed initially, omitting the [[constant of integration]] <math>+ C</math> both because this was done historically, and because it drops out when computing the definite integral.

Integrating <math display="inline">\int x^m (\log x)^n\,dx</math> by substituting <math display="inline">u = (\log x)^n</math> and <math display="inline">dv=x^m\,dx</math> yields:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\int x^m (\log x)^n\,dx
& = \frac{x^{m+1}(\log x)^n}{m+1} - \frac{n}{m+1}\int x^{m+1} \frac{(\log x)^{n-1}}{x}\,dx  \qquad\text{(for }m\neq -1\text{)}\\
& = \frac{x^{m+1}}{m+1}(\log x)^n - \frac{n}{m+1}\int x^m (\log x)^{n-1}\,dx  \qquad\text{(for }m\neq -1\text{)}
\end{align}
</math>

(also in the [[list of integrals of logarithmic functions]]). This reduces the power on the logarithm in the integrand by 1 (from <math>n</math> to <math>n-1</math>) and thus one can compute the integral [[mathematical induction|inductively]], as
<math display="block">
\int x^m (\log x)^n\,dx
= \frac{x^{m+1}}{m+1}
 \cdot \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i \frac{(n)_i}{(m+1)^i} (\log x)^{n-i}</math>

where <math display="inline">(n)_i</math> denotes the [[falling factorial]]; there is a finite sum because the induction stops at 0, since {{mvar|n}} is an integer.

In this case <math display="inline">m=n</math>, and they are integers, so

<math display="block">\int x^n (\log x)^n\,dx
= \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}
 \cdot \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i \frac{(n)_i}{(n+1)^i} (\log x)^{n-i}.</math>

Integrating from 0 to 1, all the terms vanish except the last term at 1,<ref group="note">All the terms vanish at 0 because <math display="inline">\lim_{x \to 0^+} x^m (\log x)^n  =  0</math> by [[l'Hôpital's rule]] (Bernoulli omitted this technicality), and all but the last term vanish at 1 since {{math|1=log 1 = 0}}.</ref> which yields:

<math display="block">\int_0^1 \frac{x^n (\log x)^n}{n!}\,dx
= \frac{1}{n!}\frac{1^{n+1}}{n+1}
 (-1)^n \frac{(n)_n}{(n+1)^n} = (-1)^n (n+1)^{-(n+1)}.</math>

This is equivalent to computing Euler's integral identity <math>\Gamma(n+1) = n!</math> for the [[Gamma function]] on a different domain (corresponding to changing variables by substitution), as Euler's identity itself can also be computed via an analogous integration by parts.
